question: Which statement best describes The document frame?
options: `<code>` marks a short fragment of computer code, such as a property name. It usually uses a monospace font. It is like switching to a typewriter face for a command. For multiple lines of code, place code inside `<pre>` so the spacing and line breaks are preserved. For example, wrap a short command in code, and use pre for a multi-line example. In a real page, place a block of code in pre so its spaces and line breaks remain.

`<strong>` marks text with strong importance, seriousness, or urgency. Browsers often display it in bold, but the meaning is more than a visual weight. It is like emphasizing a warning in a spoken instruction. Use it for genuinely important words, not every phrase you want to look darker. For example, mark a safety warning as important, then use CSS to make it visually prominent. In a real page, use strong to mark an urgent instruction, not merely any bold label.

`<em>` marks stress emphasis that can change how a sentence is read. Browsers often display it in italics. It is like changing your voice to emphasize one word. Use it where the emphasis affects meaning, and use CSS when you only want an italic visual style. For example, emphasize a word when it changes how a sentence should be understood. In a real page, emphasis can change the stress in a sentence, not just its font style.

`<b>` and `<i>` can draw attention or mark alternate voice without adding strong importance or stress. Their exact use depends on the text. They are like a visual annotation rather than a warning. Prefer semantic elements when the meaning is important, and do not choose tags only for their default appearance. For example, use CSS italics for a title style when no alternate voice or semantic meaning is intended. In a real page, use code for a short property name that readers may copy.
explanation: `<strong>` marks text with strong importance, seriousness, or urgency. Browsers often display it in bold, but the meaning is more than a visual weight. It is like emphasizing a warning in a spoken instruction. Use it for genuinely important words, not every phrase you want to look darker. For example, mark a safety warning as important, then use CSS to make it visually prominent. In a real page, use strong to mark an urgent instruction, not merely any bold label.
